content.text:
**Short answer:** It's a decent offer, but it isn't strong enough to justify leaving a job you're happy in. You should negotiate. You have more leverage than most candidates because Google approached you, you weren't looking, and you're fine staying where you are.

## How the offer actually compares

**Your Meta pay for the next 12 months is closer to $476K than $526K.** That's your $240K base, plus the $36K bonus, plus the $200K that actually vests next year. Any new refresh grant you get would add a little in year 1 and more after that.

**Google's year-1 pay depends on the vesting schedule, and I couldn't confirm which one you'd get.** Sources disagree. Levels.fyi lists two front-loaded options:
33% in year 1, 33% in year 2, 22% in year 3, 12% in year 4

split. **Ask the recruiter for the exact schedule in writing.** It makes a big difference:

| Schedule | Yr-1 stock | Yr-1 total (base + bonus + stock) |
|---|---|---|
| 25/25/25/25 | $270K | **$552K** |
| 33/33/22/12 | $356K | **$638K** |
| 50/28/12/10 | $540K | **$822K** |

Over 4 years the new-hire package averages about **$552K a year** before any refreshes, assuming the stock price stays flat. That's only about 5% above your $526K run-rate at Meta. With a front-loaded schedule, years 3–4 will drop unless refreshes fill the gap, and refreshes aren't guaranteed. Meta's aren't guaranteed either.

**Other things to notice:**
- **The base is a pay cut.** $235K is below your current $240K. It's above the middle of the posted range (about $227K) but well under the $271K maximum.
- **There's no sign-on bonus.** That matters if leaving means giving up an upcoming Meta bonus payout or a refresh grant that's about to start.
- **The bonus percentage is fixed by level,** so don't spend negotiating effort on it.
- **For context:** Levels.fyi puts the
median yearly compensation package for Google PMs in the SF Bay Area at $510K

. That covers all levels, though, so it's only a rough guide. Your offer is at or a bit above market for L6, not top of band.

## What I'd ask for

Give one clear counteroffer, framed around staying put: *"I'm happy at Meta and wasn't looking. I'm excited about this role, but to make the move I'd need the following."*

1. **Base: $255–260K.** That's inside the posted range and a real raise over Meta. Expect them to land somewhere around $245–255K.
2. **New-hire RSUs: $1.35–1.4M** (about $340–350K a year on average). This is the biggest lever. Your argument is that the current grant is barely above your Meta run-rate, and switching carries risk: new team, ramp-up time, and no guaranteed refreshes.
3. **Sign-on bonus: $50–100K.** Tie it to specific things you'd give up, such as your next Meta bonus payout or a recent refresh grant. Concrete numbers work better than general asks.

If they agree to all of it, year-1 pay would be roughly $650K+ on even vesting, and the 4-year average would be around $620K. That's a meaningful step up. Expect partial movement, not everything.

**Walk-away logic:** If Google won't move at all, you'd be trading a job you like for about a 5% raise plus refresh risk. For someone who cares a lot about comp, that's arguably not enough. If they improve the package meaningfully (say a 4-year average of $590K or more), I'd accept.

**Other tactics:**
- Don't share your Meta numbers in detail beyond what's needed to explain why you're asking.
- Consider mentioning the offer to your Meta manager. A retention counteroffer is possible, but only do this if you'd actually be fine staying either way.

**Yes, I'd take it, as long as you're comfortable with the non-money tradeoffs.** It clears the bar I suggested last time (a 4-year average of about $590K or more), and the improvement is real.

## The numbers

| | Google (final) | Meta (staying) |
|---|---|---|
| Base | $240K | $240K |
| Bonus | $48K (20% target) | ~$36K |
| Stock (avg/yr) | $320K | ~$250K run-rate (~$200K next 12 months) |
| **Annual total** | **~$608K** | **~$526K run-rate / ~$476K next 12 months** |

- **That's about $82K a year more than your Meta run-rate (+16%),** or roughly $330K more over 4 years before taxes and refreshes.
- **Year 1 is better still: about $132K more** than the ~$476K you'd actually earn at Meta in the next 12 months.
- **Don't count the $200K twice.** You give up that $200K of Meta stock, but it's already included in the $476K Meta figure above. The year-1 comparison has already accounted for it, so it isn't an extra cost on top.

## Check this before signing

**1. Vesting schedule.** The 4-year average is ~$608K under any schedule, but the shape changes a lot:

| Schedule | Yr 1 | Yr 2 | Yr 3 | Yr 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 25/25/25/25 | $608K | $608K | $608K | $608K |
| 33/33/22/12 | $710K | $710K | $570K | $442K |
| 50/28/12/10 | $928K | $646K | $442K | $416K |

With a front-loaded schedule, years 3–4 fall below your Meta pay unless refreshes fill the gap. Refreshes aren't guaranteed, so plan your budget around the base grant, not the year-1 peak.

**2. Stock price.** The $1.28M is a dollar amount. Ask how it converts to shares (which date or average price) so you know what you're actually getting.

**3. Timing your exit from Meta.** Meta stock usually vests quarterly. Ask for a start date just after your next Meta vest, and after any bonus payout if one is close. Delaying the start costs Google nothing, so recruiters almost always agree even after a "best offer." It may be worth tens of thousands of dollars to you. It's the one thing I'd still ask for.

## Don't push further on money

They've already moved on base (+$5K) and stock (+$200K). They've also said this is their best offer. Asking again for a sign-on bonus probably won't work and could cost you some goodwill. Ask about the start date, then accept.

## The non-money question

Money is the only area where this offer clearly wins. You're happy at Meta, and a new job brings a new team, time to ramp up, and the risk that refreshes don't come. If comp really matters most to you, ~16% more each year (and much more in year 1 if vesting is front-loaded) is a strong reason to switch. Only tell your Meta manager about the offer if you'd honestly be happy staying for a matching counteroffer. Otherwise you're just delaying a decision you've already made.
